claim: SF3B1 is the most frequently mutated gene in patients with MDS.
source: SF3B1 is the most frequently mutated gene in patients with MDS (Yoshida et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yoshida et al., 2011

claim: Mutations in SF3B1 can lead to widespread changes in splicing.
source: Even though reports have shown that mutations in SF3B1 can lead to widespread changes in splicing (Inoue and Abdel-Wahab, 2016), the exact pathways that are disrupted and lead to the pathogenesis of ineffective hematopoiesis and carcinogenesis in MDS and AML are not yet fully elucidated.
evidence: Supported by citation to Inoue and Abdel-Wahab, 2016

claim: The innate immune signaling pathways have been shown to be activated in MDS and AML.
source: The innate immune signaling pathways have been shown to be activated in MDS and AML (Barreyro et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barreyro et al., 2018

claim: The upstream activation of toll like receptors (TLRs), interleukin receptor 1 receptor accessory protein (IL1RAP), and interleukin 8 (IL8) activate the IRAK/TRAF6 pathways and lead to NF-kB activation.
source: The upstream activation of toll like receptors (TLRs), interleukin receptor 1 receptor accessory protein (IL1RAP), and interleukin 8 (IL8) activate the IRAK/TRAF6 pathways and lead to NF-kB activation (Mitchell et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mitchell et al., 2018

claim: U2AF1 splicing factor mutation can lead to retention of exon 4 leading to overexpression of IRAK4 in MDS and AML.
source: We had recently shown that another splicing mutation in U2AF1 splicing factor can lead to retention of exon 4 leading to overexpression of IRAK4 in MDS and AML (Smith et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith et al., 2019

claim: SF3B1 mutation leads to exon 6 retention leading to overexpression of active isoform of IRAK4 known as IRAK4-long (IRAK4-L).
source: In the present report, we now demonstrate that SF3B1 mutation leads to exon 6 retention leading to overexpression of active isoform of IRAK4 known as IRAK4-long (IRAK4-L).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by RNA-seq and RT-PCR data presented in Figure 1

claim: RNA-seq splicing analysis of SF3B1 mutant MDS samples revealed retention of full-length exon 6 of IRAK4.
source: RNA-seq splicing analysis of SF3B1 mutant MDS samples revealed retention of full-length exon 6 of IRAK4, a critical downstream mediator that links the Myddosome to inflammatory NF-kB activation.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Analysis of RNA-seq of purified CD34+ HSPCs from HC and SF3B1 mutant MDS samples demonstrated an increased retention of full length exon 6 of IRAK4 in the SF3B1 mutant samples.
source: Analysis of RNA-seq of purified CD34+ HSPCs from HC and SF3B1 mutant MDS samples demonstrated an increased retention of full length exon 6 of IRAK4 in the SF3B1 mutant samples (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and Sashimi plots shown in Figure 1A

claim: The full length retention of exon 6 was confirmed by RT-PCR in a larger cohort of primary samples demonstrating a significantly greater ratio of long isoform of IRAK4 in SF3B1 mutant samples when compared to HC and MDS patients without splicing mutations.
source: The full length retention of exon 6 was confirmed by RT-PCR in a larger cohort of primary samples demonstrating a significantly greater ratio of long isoform of IRAK4 in SF3B1 mutant samples when compared to HC and MDS patients without splicing mutations (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B and C

claim: Transfection of mutant SF3B1-K700E into HEK293-IRAK4exon6 cells resulted in inclusion of IRAK4 exon 6 from the splicing reporter compared to SF3B1-WT or vector-transfected HEK293-IRAK4exon6 cells.
source: Transfection of mutant SF3B1-K700E into HEK293-IRAK4exon6 cells resulted in inclusion of IRAK4 exon 6 from the splicing reporter compared to SF3B1-WT or vector-transfected HEK293-IRAK4exon6 cells (Figure 1D), indicating that SF3B1-K700E directly mediates inclusion of IRAK4 exon 6.
evidence: Supported by splicing reporter assay data shown in Figure 1D

claim: SF3B1-K700E directly mediates inclusion of IRAK4 exon 6.
source: Transfection of mutant SF3B1-K700E into HEK293-IRAK4exon6 cells resulted in inclusion of IRAK4 exon 6 from the splicing reporter compared to SF3B1-WT or vector-transfected HEK293-IRAK4exon6 cells (Figure 1D), indicating that SF3B1-K700E directly mediates inclusion of IRAK4 exon 6.
evidence: Inferred from splicing reporter assay data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Full length IRAK4 protein (IRAK4-L) is composed of a death domain, hinge region, and a kinase domain.
source: Full length IRAK4 protein (IRAK4-L) is composed of a death domain, hinge region, and a kinase domain (Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on established protein structure knowledge and illustrated in Figure 2A

claim: Exon 6 encodes a part of the kinase domain of IRAK4 protein.
source: Exon 6 encodes a part of the kinase domain of IRAK4 protein.
evidence: Based on protein structure analysis and sequence information

claim: Plasmid with the full length exon 6 led to stable expression of IRAK4-long protein and resulted into increased phosphorylation of p65 when compared to the smaller isoforms.
source: Immunoblotting analysis showed that plasmid with the full length exon 6 led to stable expression of IRAK4-long protein and resulted into increased phosphorylation of p65 when compared to the smaller isoforms (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Transfection of IRAK4 S1 and S2 constructs led to generation of lower molecular weight IRAK4 proteins with decreased expression when compared to the longer isoform.
source: By contrast, transfection of IRAK4 S1 and S2 constructs led to generation of lower molecular weight IRAK4 proteins with decreased expression when compared to the longer isoform (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Treatment with proteasome inhibitor (MG132) led to increased expression of the smaller IRAK4 bands demonstrating that these were targeted for proteasomal degradation.
source: Treatment with proteasome inhibitor (MG132) led to increased expression of the smaller IRAK4 bands demonstrating that these were targeted for proteasomal degradation (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data with MG132 treatment shown in Figure 2C

claim: Immunoprecipitation in HEK293T cells transfected with IRAK4-L, S1, S2, and HA-tagged Lys48 linked in presence of proteasome inhibitor MG132 demonstrated an increased association of Lys48 linked ubiquitin chains with shorter IRAK4 isoforms, validating ubiquitin mediated degradation.
source: Immunoprecipitation in HEK293T cells transfected with IRAK4-L, S1, S2, and HA-tagged Lys48 linked in presence of proteasome inhibitor MG132 demonstrated an increased association of Lys48 linked ubiquitin chains with shorter IRAK4 isoforms, validating ubiquitin mediated degradation (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Isogenic cells with SF3B1 K700E mutation demonstrated overexpression of IRAK4-L and higher activation of p-p65.
source: Isogenic cells with WT and K700E mutation of SF3B1 were evaluated and the mutant cells demonstrated overexpression of IRAK4-L and higher activation of p-p65 (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data from isogenic cells shown in Figure 2E

claim: The IRAK4-long containing the death domain was able to associate with MYD88 in immunoprecipitation experiments, while the shorter isoforms did not.
source: Finally, we showed that the IRAK4-long containing the death domain was able to associate with MYD88 in immunoprecipitation experiments, while the shorter isoforms did not; thus, providing the mechanistic basis of activation seen only with the IRAK4-long isoform (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2F

claim: The association of IRAK4-long with MYD88 provides the mechanistic basis of activation seen only with the IRAK4-long isoform.
source: Finally, we showed that the IRAK4-long containing the death domain was able to associate with MYD88 in immunoprecipitation experiments, while the shorter isoforms did not; thus, providing the mechanistic basis of activation seen only with the IRAK4-long isoform (Figure 2F).
evidence: Inferred from immunoprecipitation data and known role of MYD88-IRAK4 interaction in signaling

claim: Signal transduction via TLRs is primarily mediated by IRAK4-TRAF6 activation.
source: Signal transduction via TLRs is primarily mediated by IRAK4-TRAF6 activation and TRAF6 is an E3 ligase that conjugates ubiquitin chains to itself and its substrates.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of TLR signaling pathways

claim: TRAF6 is an E3 ligase that conjugates ubiquitin chains to itself and its substrates.
source: Signal transduction via TLRs is primarily mediated by IRAK4-TRAF6 activation and TRAF6 is an E3 ligase that conjugates ubiquitin chains to itself and its substrates.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of TRAF6 function

claim: The consensus sequence of TRAF6 binding motif is P(P-2)XE(P0)XX(Acidic/Aromatic)(P+3) and is present in known TRAF6 substrates.
source: The consensus sequence of TRAF6 binding motif is P(P-2)XE(P0)XX(Acidic/Aromatic)(P+3) and is present in known TRAF6 substrates (Figure 3A).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of TRAF6 binding motif and shown in Figure 3A

claim: CDK2 could be a potential substrate of TRAF6.
source: Since MDS/AML are characterized by ineffective hematopoiesis due to block in myeloid differentiation, we performed a search for the TRAF6 motif in cell cycle regulators and determined that CDK2 could be a potential substrate (Figure 3A).
evidence: Inferred from sequence analysis showing TRAF6 binding motif in CDK2

claim: Structural modeling of TRAF6 and CDK2 peptide show that positions P-2, P0, and P3 in CDK2 correspond to three distinct sub-pockets in the binding site of TRAF6 and supports the notion that CDK2 can be ubiquitinated by TRAF6.
source: Structural modeling of TRAF6 and CDK2 peptide show that positions P-2, P0, and P3 in CDK2 correspond to three distinct sub-pockets in the binding site of TRAF6 and supports the notion that CDK2 can be ubiquitinated by TRAF6 (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by computational docking studies shown in Figure 3B

claim: CDK2 was associated with a much stronger K63 ubiquitin that was dependent on TRAF6 and IRAK4 overexpression.
source: To directly test the role of TRAF6 dependent ubiquitination of CDK2 in chronic innate immune signaling, we ectopically expressed CDK2, IRAK4, and TRAF6 in presence of either Lys48 linked ubiquitin or Lys63 linked ubiquitin.CDK2 was associated with a much stronger K63 ubiquitin that was dependent on TRAF6 and IRAK4 overexpression (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3C

claim: TRAF6 mediated Lys63 linked ubiquitination was decreased in CDK2 mutants as compared to wild type CDK2.
source: To validate this result, we generated alanine and glycine mutants (CDK2 Myc 122 and CDK2 Myc 123) within CDK2 binding site of TRAF6 and examined their ubiquitination in presence of IRAK4-L and TRAF6 by immunoprecipitating CDK2. Immunoblotting analysis show that TRAF6 mediated Lys63 linked ubiquitination was decreased in CDK2 mutants as compared to wild type CDK2 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data with CDK2 mutants shown in Figure 3D

claim: Isogenic cell line containing SF3B1 K700E mutant contained heavily K63 ubiquitin CDK2.
source: Furthermore, we used isogenic cell line containing SF3B1 K700E mutant and K700K control and demonstrated that the mutant cells contained heavily K63 ubiquitin CDK2 (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data from isogenic cells shown in Figure 3E

claim: Treatment with CDK2 inhibitors in vitro led to increased hematopoietic colony formation and increased myeloid differentiation in SF3B1 mutant MDS cases.
source: Cases of MDS with SF3B1 mutations are characterized by ineffective hematopoiesis and treatment with CDK2 inhibitors in vitro led to increased hematopoietic colony formation and increased myeloid differentiation as evident by CD14 expression seen in three primary samples. (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 3F

claim: CA4948 treatment is able to inhibit downstream NF-kB activation upon TLR engagement in leukemic THP1 cells.
source: CA4948 treatment is able to inhibit downstream NF-kB activation upon TLR engagement in leukemic THP1 cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4B

claim: IRAK4 inhibitor led to reduction in cytokine production in leukemic cells after engagements of Myd88/TLR pathways.
source: This IRAK4 inhibitor also led to reduction in cytokine production in leukemic cells after engagements of Myd88/TLR pathways (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by mRNA expression data shown in Figure 4C

claim: IRAK4 inhibition led to a significant increase in myeloid colonies as well as increase in myeloid differentiation markers in MDS samples with SF3B1 mutation.
source: Bone marrow mononuclear cells from MDS patients with SF3B1 mutation were cultured in the presence and absence of the IRAK4 inhibitor in vitro and then colonies were assessed by flow cytometry for myeloid differentiation. We observed a significant increase in myeloid colonies as well as increase in myeloid differentiation markers after IRAK4 inhibition in three distinct samples (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by clonogenic assay and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Treatment of healthy human CD34 stem and progenitor cells with IRAK4 inhibitor did not lead to any significant changes in colony numbers.
source: Treatment of healthy human CD34 stem and progenitor cells with IRAK4 inhibitor did not lead to any significant changes in colony numbers (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 4E

claim: IRAK4 knockdown with siRNAs in a primary MDS sample with SF3B1 mutations led to an increase in colonies and myeloid differentiation.
source: We also performed IRAK4 knockdown with siRNAs in a primary MDS sample with SF3B1 mutations and observed an increase in colonies and myeloid differentiation upon knockdown, validating IRAK4 as a target for relieving the differentiation block seen in MDS (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by siRNA knockdown and clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Cohort with higher IRAK4-long expression had lower platelet counts, higher RBC transfusion needs and higher leukemic blast counts, all indicative of worse clinical features.
source: IRAK4-long expression was determined from an existing expression dataset from selected CD34+ cells and used to divide the cohort into high and low IRAK4 based on median expression. We observed that cohort with higher IRAK4-long expression had lower platelet counts, higher RBC transfusion needs and higher leukemic blast counts, all indicative of worse clinical features (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by analysis of clinical data from 183 MDS samples shown in Figure 5A

claim: Treatment with IRAK4 inhibitor led to decrease in MDS cells after 3–4 weeks of treatment in five distinct samples.
source: Next, we established xenografts with MDS samples with SF3B1 mutation and treated the NSG mice with either IRAK4 inhibitor (CA4948) and placebo controls. Treatment with IRAK4 inhibitor led to decrease in MDS cells after 3–4 weeks of treatment in five distinct samples (Figure 5B–D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by xenograft data shown in Figure 5B-D and supplementary figures

claim: IRAK4-long was found to be elevated in selected cases of AML HSCs, most significantly in adverse risk patients with complex cytogenetics.
source: Since innate immune signaling pathways have been shown to play roles in leukemic stem cell propagation (Barreyro et al., 2018), we next evaluated IRAK4-long expression in a dataset derived from sorted AML/MDS HSCs and HC (Barreyro et al., 2012). IRAK4-long was found to be elevated in selected cases of AML HSCs, most significantly in adverse risk patients with complex cytogenetics (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by analysis of sorted HSC data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Transcriptomic signature of IRAK4 overexpression showed significant concordance with a published leukemic stem cell signature.
source: Consistent with this finding, we derived a transcriptomic signature of IRAK4 overexpression from 183 MDS samples (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and compared it to a published leukemic stem cell signature (Eppert et al., 2011) and found significant concordance (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5F comparing to Eppert et al., 2011

claim: IRAK4 inhibition led to reduced MDS clones in secondary transplants, demonstrating decrease in disease initiating activity.
source: Lastly, we tested the efficacy of IRAK4 inhibition in disease initiation in vivo. IRAK4 inhibitor and placebo treated xenograft mice were sacrificed and cells used for secondary xenografts. IRAK4 inhibition led to reduced MDS clones in secondary transplants, demonstrating decrease in disease initiating activity (Figure 5G and H, Figure 5—figure supplement 3, summarized in Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by secondary xenograft data shown in Figure 5G-H and supplementary figures

claim: Mutations in splicing genes are one of the most common alterations in MDS and AML and predominantly affect SF3B1, U2AF1, and SRSF2.
source: Mutations in splicing genes are one of the most common alterations in MDS and AML and predominantly affect SF3B1, U2AF1, and SRSF2 (1).
evidence: Supported by citation (reference 1 in the text)

claim: SF3B1 can be mutated in solid tumors such as breast cancer, melanoma, and others.
source: SF3B1 is the most commonly mutated splicing gene in MDS and can also be mutated in solid tumors such as breast cancer, melanoma, and others (Papaemmanuil et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Papaemmanuil et al., 2013

claim: Mutant U2AF1 (S34F) directly regulates IRAK4 exon 4 retention in MDS/AML, which results in expression of the longer IRAK4 isoform (IRAK4-L).
source: We recently demonstrated that mutant U2AF1 (S34F) directly regulates IRAK4 exon 4 retention in MDS/AML, which results in expression of the longer IRAK4 isoform (IRAK4-L) (Smith et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith et al., 2019

claim: SF3B1 mutations lead to production of active IRAK4-L isoforms by aberrant retention of exon 6.
source: In the present report, we demonstrate that SF3B1 mutations also lead to production of active IRAK4-L isoforms but by aberrant retention of exon 6 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data throughout the manuscript

claim: The functional activation of the IRAK4 pathway by two different exon retention events by U2AF1 mutations and SF3B1 mutations suggest that this is an important functional event in MDS pathobiology.
source: The functional activation of the IRAK4 pathway by two different exon retention events by U2AF1 mutations and SF3B1 mutations suggest that this is an important functional event in MDS pathobiology.
evidence: Inferred from the convergence of two different splicing mutations on the same pathway

claim: Innate immune signaling mediators such as IL1RAP, IL8/CXCR2, TLRs as well as myeloid derived suppressor cells are activated in MDS.
source: Recent work has shown that innate immune signaling mediators such as IL1RAP, IL8/CXCR2, TLRs as well as myeloid derived suppressor cells are activated in MDS (Barreyro et al., 2012; Dimicoli et al., 2013; Wei et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2013; Rhyasen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Interaction of IRAK4 with upstream TLR/MyD88 pathways is critical in MDS pathogenesis.
source: Our findings further support the role of activated innate immune signaling pathways in MDS and suggest that interaction of IRAK4 with upstream TLR/MyD88 pathways is critical in MDS pathogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing IRAK4-MYD88 interaction and downstream effects

claim: Overexpression of active IRAK4 isoforms in splicing mutant MDS suggests that these cells are primed to respond to upstream TLR and MyD88 activation.
source: Demonstration of overexpression of active IRAK4 isoforms in splicing mutant MDS suggests that these cells are primed to respond to upstream TLR and MyD88 activation.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing IRAK4-L overexpression and its interaction with MYD88

claim: Active IRAK4 isoforms potentially represent a shared downstream functional pathway that regulates MDS/AML malignant cell survival in different spliceosome mutant subsets.
source: In fact, since active IRAK4 isoforms are expressed in different spliceosome mutant subsets, they potentially represent a shared downstream functional pathway that regulates MDS/AML malignant cell survival.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both U2AF1 and SF3B1 mutations lead to IRAK4-L expression

claim: CA-4948 is a specific inhibitor of IRAK4 that is now being tested in clinical trials in MDS/AML and lymphomas.
source: CA-4948 is a specific inhibitor of IRAK4 that is now being tested in clinical trials in MDS/AML and lymphomas (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04278768; NCT03328078) and in preliminary findings has shown a tolerable safety profile.
evidence: Supported by reference to clinical trial identifiers

claim: CA-4948 has shown a tolerable safety profile in preliminary findings.
source: CA-4948 is a specific inhibitor of IRAK4 that is now being tested in clinical trials in MDS/AML and lymphomas (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04278768; NCT03328078) and in preliminary findings has shown a tolerable safety profile.
evidence: Based on preliminary clinical trial data

claim: Early clinical data appears encouraging in spliceosome mutant patients, supporting the validity of IRAK4 as a therapeutic target in SF3B1 mutant MDS/AML.
source: Early clinical data appears encouraging in spliceosome mutant patients, supporting the validity of IRAK4 as a therapeutic target in SF3B1 mutant MDS/AML (Garcia-Manero et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Garcia-Manero et al., 2021

claim: CA4948 shows inhibitory activity against FLT3 and CLKs.
source: CA4948 also shows inhibitory activity against FLT3 and CLKs, potentially another reason for the antimalignant activity observed in our preclinical studies.
evidence: Based on known properties of CA4948

claim: Inhibiting IRAK4 pharmacologically leads to shrinkage of the MDS/AML clones in vivo.
source: Our data suggests that inhibiting IRAK4 pharmacologically leads to shrinkage of the MDS/AML clones in vivo and this correlates with decreased blast counts seen with CA4948 monotherapy in relapsed/refractory MDS/AML in early results.
evidence: Supported by xenograft data presented in the study

claim: Decreased blast counts are seen with CA4948 monotherapy in relapsed/refractory MDS/AML in early results.
source: Our data suggests that inhibiting IRAK4 pharmacologically leads to shrinkage of the MDS/AML clones in vivo and this correlates with decreased blast counts seen with CA4948 monotherapy in relapsed/refractory MDS/AML in early results.
evidence: Based on early clinical trial results

claim: MDS/AML are characterized by block in hematopoietic differentiation that leads to neutropenia and subsequent infections.
source: MDS/AML are characterized by block in hematopoietic differentiation that leads to neutropenia and subsequent infections.
evidence: Based on established clinical knowledge of MDS/AML

claim: IRAK4 inhibition promotes myeloid differentiation in SF3B1 mutant cases.
source: Our data suggests that IRAK4 inhibition promotes myeloid differentiation in SF3B1 mutant cases.
evidence: Supported by in vitro differentiation data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Exon 6 retention leads to a longer isoform, encoding a protein (IRAK4-long) that contains the entire death domain and kinase domain, leading to maximal activation of NF-kB.
source: Exon 6 retention leads to a longer isoform, encoding a protein (IRAK4-long) that contains the entire death domain and kinase domain, leading to maximal activation of NF-kB.
evidence: Supported by protein structure analysis and NF-kB activation data shown in Figure 2

claim: Cells with wild-type SF3B1 contain smaller IRAK4 isoforms that are targeted for proteasomal degradation.
source: Cells with wild-type SF3B1 contain smaller IRAK4 isoforms that are targeted for proteasomal degradation.
evidence: Supported by proteasome inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 2C and ubiquitination data in Figure 2D

claim: Expression of IRAK4-long in SF3B1 mutant cells induces TRAF6 activation leading to K63-linked ubiquitination of CDK2, associated with a block in hematopoietic differentiation.
source: Expression of IRAK4-long in SF3B1 mutant cells induces TRAF6 activation leading to K63-linked ubiquitination of CDK2, associated with a block in hematopoietic differentiation.
evidence: Supported by ubiquitination data in Figure 3 and differentiation assays

claim: Inhibition of IRAK4 with CA-4948 leads to reduction in NF-kB activation, inflammatory cytokine production, enhanced myeloid differentiation in vitro and reduced leukemic growth in xenograft models.
source: Inhibition of IRAK4 with CA-4948, leads to reduction in NF-kB activation, inflammatory cytokine production, enhanced myeloid differentiation in vitro and reduced leukemic growth in xenograft models.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 4 and 5

claim: IRAK4 is a critical downstream mediator that links the Myddosome to inflammatory NF-kB activation.
source: RNA-seq splicing analysis of SF3B1 mutant MDS samples revealed retention of full-length exon 6 of IRAK4, a critical downstream mediator that links the Myddosome to inflammatory NF-kB activation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of IRAK4 function in innate immune signaling

claim: The exclusion of mRNA sequence encoding amino acids 188–217 in exon 6 as seen in HC can lead to two possible smaller IRAK4 isoforms.
source: The exclusion of mRNA sequence encoding amino acids 188–217 in exon 6 as seen in HC can lead to two possible smaller IRAK4 isoforms.
evidence: Inferred from sequence analysis and shown in Figure 2A

claim: Isoform S1 (191 amino acids) could be produced due to formation of a premature stop codon (TGA) leading to a smaller IRAK4 isoform containing death, hinge, and part of kinase domain.
source: Isoform S1 (191 amino acids) could be produced due to formation of a premature stop codon (TGA) leading to a smaller IRAK4 isoform containing death, hinge, and part of kinase domain.
evidence: Inferred from sequence analysis shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Isoform S2 (243 amino acids) could be generated by utilizing an alternative translational start site (ATG) resulting in an IRAK4 isoform with only the kinase domain.
source: Isoform S2 (243 amino acids) (S2) could also be generated by utilizing an alternative translational start site (ATG) resulting in an IRAK4 isoform with only the kinase domain (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from sequence analysis shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Innate immune signaling pathways have been shown to play roles in leukemic stem cell propagation.
source: Since innate immune signaling pathways have been shown to play roles in leukemic stem cell propagation (Barreyro et al., 2018), we next evaluated IRAK4-long expression in a dataset derived from sorted AML/MDS HSCs and HC (Barreyro et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barreyro et al., 2018

claim: MDS and AML are frequently incurable hematologic disorders characterized by cytopenia that are a major cause of morbidity and mortality.
source: MDS and AML are frequently incurable hematologic disorders characterized by cytopenia that are a major cause of morbidity and mortality.
evidence: Based on established clinical knowledge

claim: K63 ubiquitination leads to increased protein stability and interactions.
source: Furthermore, we used isogenic cell line containing SF3B1 K700E mutant and K700K control and demonstrated that the mutant cells contained heavily K63 ubiquitin CDK2 (Figure 3E). Since K63 ubiquitination leads to increased protein stability and interactions, we tested whether inhibiting CDK2 would lead to functional effects in patient samples containing the SF3B1 mutation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of K63 ubiquitination function

claim: Cases of MDS with SF3B1 mutations are characterized by ineffective hematopoiesis.
source: Cases of MDS with SF3B1 mutations are characterized by ineffective hematopoiesis and treatment with CDK2 inhibitors in vitro led to increased hematopoietic colony formation and increased myeloid differentiation as evident by CD14 expression seen in three primary samples.
evidence: Based on established clinical knowledge of SF3B1 mutant MDS

claim: The hallmark of MDS and AML is a block in differentiation leading to dysplastic maturation and cytopenia.
source: The hallmark of MDS and AML is a block in differentiation leading to dysplastic maturation and cytopenia.
evidence: Based on established clinical knowledge

claim: CA4948 binds to the kinase domain on the IRAK4 protein.
source: We wanted to evaluate the efficacy of IRAK4 inhibition in SF3B1 mutated MDS with a clinically relevant inhibitor, CA4948 (Emavusertib), which binds to the kinase domain on the protein (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 4A
